label: A_shipped
text:
The alley was a vein of cool stone, narrow enough that my shoulders brushed the mossy walls on both sides. The enchanted lanterns hung like dying stars, their brass cages tarnished green with age, their light flickering in time with something I couldn’t name. The air tasted of damp wool and old iron, the kind of scent that lingers after a downpour. My cloak caught the breeze, the fabric clinging to my arms as I moved, each step deliberate. The pendant—my mother’s—burned against my collarbone, a cold weight I couldn’t shake. Thorne’s summons still hung in the air, a leaden promise. I should have known better than to linger.

Julian’s hand was warm where it brushed mine, grounding. His fingers steadied the parchment, the wax seal glistening like a thing alive. I’d seen him use that same grip to steady himself against a wall, against me. Now it held a summons that would drag me before a tribunal that had already decided my guilt. The words *kwishif* still echoed in my skull, the scholar’s term for the Eight-born, and my fingers tightened around the pendant.

I pushed past him.

The motion was instinctive, a refusal to be held still by guilt or expectation. His shoulder was solid under my palm, the muscles shifting as he turned to follow, his voice low and pitched just for me. “You don’t have to go in alone.”

I didn’t look back. The lanterns flickered again, their glow dimming like a held breath. The alley stretched ahead, a tunnel of shifting light and shadow, the air thick with the weight of something unseen. Julian’s presence was a pressure at my back, a silent demand that I acknowledge him. I could feel his gaze on the nape of my neck, a heat that didn’t belong in the damp cold.

His voice dropped, rougher now, like gravel underfoot. “Lirael.”

The pendant caught on the inside of my collarbone. The cost wasn’t just the summons. It was the way his voice curled around my name, the way it made my stomach clench. I stopped walking. The lanterns guttered, one by one, plunging us into near-darkness. The only light came from the faintest shimmer of Julian’s skin, the Weave-Script along his forearm pulsing like a heartbeat.

“You’re afraid,” he said, and it wasn’t a question.

I swallowed. “I’m not.”

The lie tasted like ash. The lanterns flared back to life, their glow catching the silver scar that ran down the side of his hand. The scar was a remnant of a past mishap, something he’d never explained. His fingers tapped rhythmically against his thigh, the motion betraying the stillness in his shoulders.

“You always say that when you’re lying.”

The words settled into the space between us, heavy with implication. The alley felt smaller, the walls pressing in. Julian’s gaze lingered on my hands as I spoke, as if captivated by their movement, by the way they fidgeted with the edge of my cloak. The fabric had a frayed hem, the kind of detail that would have gone unnoticed if not for the way the lanterns caught it, turning it into something almost luminous.

I wanted to push past him again. I wanted to step closer. The lanterns flickered once more, their light dancing across his jaw, the stubble there catching the glow like a promise. The air smelled of burnt metal and old magic, the kind of scent that clung to places where sacrifices had been made.

Julian exhaled, slow and controlled. “You don’t have to do this.”

His voice was a low rumble, the kind that vibrated in my ribs. The lanterns dimmed again, the shadows stretching like fingers. The pendant at my throat was ice against my skin, but Julian’s presence was a fire I couldn’t ignore.

I turned to face him, the lanterns casting long shadows across his face. His eyes were a deep hazel, the kind that seemed to shift with the light, glimmering with hints of gold. The scar on his hand caught the light as he flexed his fingers, the silver catching the glow like a blade.

“Why are you here?” I asked, the words raw.

His gaze didn’t waver. “Because you asked me to be.”

The truth of it settled into the space between us, a weight neither of us could ignore. The lanterns flickered one last time, their light dying like a held breath.

The alley was silent.
